newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Rand, bullion hacks SAfrica gold mines Q1.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Rand, bullion hacks SAfrica gold mines Q1.

text.p: The double whammy of a stronger rand and weaker bullion price could hack South African gold mines' first quarter earnings by between 20 and 30 percent, some mining analysts said on Monday.
But others put the decline at a far more severe 58 percent.
The industry begins March quarter reporting on Thursday with Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd kicking off the round.
"Earnings could be down by as much as 58 percent. The steep drop in the gold price will really take its toll," said Dave Giese, analyst at Smith Borkhum Hare.
Earnings were likely to be further eroded by lower production due to four public holidays this quarter.
"My feeling is that this quarter will be a pretty poor quarter. We had additional holidays and the gold price has been much weaker than before," said Giese.
From January the bullion price suffered a meltdown brought about by anxiety over central banks' gold sales and investment funds' withdrawal from the metal.
It lost $15 in the first few days of 1997, sliding below $354 an ounce and failed to recover lost ground in the ensuing months. The gold price was on Monday last bid at a feeble $346.60.

Furthermore, the rand -- which shed 29 percent of its value against the dollar last year and carried the rand gold price to record highs -- has firmed, snatching away from mines any reprieve. The rand was last bid at 4.45 on the dollar.
Analysts said the average dollar gold price for the March quarter was likely to drop by 6.5 percent from the December quarter. The rand gold price was seen falling by 8.5 percent.

The first three months have not painted too glowing a profit picture for the rest of the year and, with the bullion price showing no signs of recovery, the South African gold mining industry seems to still face gloom, some analysts say.
But, others said that the first quarter might not set the trend for the rest of 1997.

"We've had a bad start, but it won't necessarily carry on through the rest of the year. Gold production could pick up next quarter. We just had a very bad January month," said Leon Esterhuizen, analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.

Despite first quarter production seen shrinking by between 1.5 to 2.0 percent, analysts say that output this year -- after last year's dismal 494.62 tonnes -- could still stabilise around the 500 tonne level. Some said it could even improve.

"This year's production should level out and could even show a slight improvement. Mines that had a poor 1996 are turning around and recovery potential from others could turn the downward trend and we could produce more than the 500 tonne forecast," Giese said.
While little excitement was expected from individual mines, analysts said that those which reported poor December quarters could pleasantly surprise from a recovery point of view.
Analysts were divided on Kloof Gold Mining Co Ltd with some singling it out as a possible recovery case and others saying it would be a "disaster".
Driefontein Consolidated Ltd was seen improving.
Analysts agreed that successful forward hedging mines would hold their heads above water and they cited East Rand Gold and Uranium Co Ltd.
